diagnostic_evidence.quote: the choice of basis vectors does not matter due to invariance of wedge product under change of orthonomal basis.

issues.failure_explanation: An arbitrary change of orthonormal basis need not preserve orientation: reversing one basis vector reverses the sign of $e_1\wedge\cdots\wedge e_m$. Thus a rectifiable set alone does not determine the stated current; an orientation and positively oriented tangent bases are required.

failure_location.quote: Given an $m$-Hausdorff rectifiable set $S\subset \R^{d}$, the unique current associated with it is defined as $[S]\in  \Omega_{0}^{m}(\R^{d})^{*} $

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Require an oriented rectifiable set and use positively oriented orthonormal tangent bases, or explicitly replace the construction by an orientation-independent object.
issues.overall_effect: The foundational definition of $[S]$, and consequently the orientation conventions used to define normal cycles as currents, are ill-defined as written.
issues.title: The current associated with a rectifiable set is not unique without an orientation
issues.why_classification: Adding the standard orientation datum is a local repair and leaves the later computational method intact for consistently oriented meshes.

issues.failure_explanation: The supremum defining a dual norm must be restricted to forms with norm at most one. Without that restriction, linear scaling of any form on which $[S]-[T]$ is nonzero makes the supremum infinite.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Restrict the supremum to $\{\omega:\|\omega\|_\infty\leq1\}$ and use the correctly named form space.
issues.overall_effect: The stated current distance is not a finite dual norm except when the two currents coincide, so the immediately following interpretation of it is invalid as written.
issues.title: The displayed dual norm omits the unit-ball constraint
issues.why_classification: The missing unit-ball restriction has a short, forced correction that preserves the intended discussion.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: which is a consistent approximation \cite{NCpaper}, as the edge-lengths tend to zero.

issues.failure_explanation: The cylindrical current integrates the spatially varying test form along the whole edge. Replacing it by evaluation at the edge center is explicitly introduced only as a consistent midpoint approximation, but the paper subsequently drops the approximation sign and identifies the resulting finite Dirac sum with the exact $N(\mathcal T)$. For a nonconstant spatial kernel this quadrature is not exact on a finite edge.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Keep a distinct symbol for the quadrature-discretized normal cycle, state the compression guarantees relative to that object, and separately quantify its consistency error with respect to $N(\mathcal T)$.
issues.overall_effect: The constructed object and its compression are guaranteed relative only to a quadrature-discretized surrogate, not to the exact normal cycle of the triangulation. Claims that the displayed Dirac sum is an exact decomposition are unreliable.
issues.title: A midpoint quadrature approximation is later asserted to equal the exact normal cycle
issues.why_classification: The core compression remains usable, but a complete repair requires distinguishing approximation layers and weakens the advertised exact representation of the triangulated normal cycle.

issues.failure_explanation: The cylindrical derivation yields a coefficient $\pi/2$ in magnitude, while the assembled decomposition uses $\pi$. Its induced edge-edge inner product therefore has coefficient $\pi^2$, not the $\pi^2/4$ claimed in the earlier metric formula. The subsequent real embedding also changes only the boundary coefficient to $\pi/2$, so it is not the image of the displayed $NC_delta$ construction.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Reconcile the normalization throughout the cylindrical and spherical derivations, $NC_delta$, and $realembedding$, and verify that the resulting inner product reproduces $NC_disc_met$.
issues.overall_effect: At least one of the Dirac representation, the real-valued embedding, and the claimed agreement with the discrete normal-cycle metric has the wrong scale, so compressed distances and weights do not represent the stated metric.
issues.title: The assembled Dirac decomposition has inconsistent normalization factors
issues.why_classification: The inconsistency concerns fixed scalar factors and can be repaired locally without changing the compression architecture or its asymptotic guarantees.

issues.failure_explanation: If $u=e_1(x,u)\times e_2(x,u)$, the coefficient of the basis bivector $e_1\wedge e_3$ is $a_1b_3-a_3b_1=-u_2$, not $+u_2$. The resulting spherical weight therefore has an incorrect second coordinate under the basis convention explicitly used in the source.

failure_location.quote: \tau_{x,u} = u_{1}\begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ e_2  \end{pmatrix}\wedge  \begin{pmatrix} 0\\ e_3 \end{pmatrix} + u_{2}\begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ e_1  \end{pmatrix}\wedge  \begin{pmatrix} 0\\ e_3 \end{pmatrix} + u_{3}\begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ e_1  \end{pmatrix}\wedge  \begin{pmatrix} 0\\ e_2 \end{pmatrix}

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace the middle term by $-u_2(e_1\wedge e_3)$, or equivalently choose the cyclic basis $e_3\wedge e_1$ and propagate that basis convention through the weights and real embedding.
issues.overall_effect: Boundary Dirac weights, and hence boundary contributions to the compressed normal-cycle metric, can have the wrong sign in one coordinate.
issues.title: The spherical bivector coordinate expansion has the wrong sign
issues.why_classification: This is a local basis-sign correction that preserves all substantive constructions once propagated consistently.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: Fix domain $\mathcal{X}$, $m \ll n$, RKHS $V$, RKHS kernel function $k:\mathcal{X}\times \mathcal{X} \longrightarrow \R$

issues.failure_explanation: An RKHS kernel is only required to be positive semidefinite, so distinct control points do not imply that $K_{CC}$ is invertible. For example, a constant kernel gives a rank-one matrix for any $m>1$. The algorithm and theorem therefore use an undefined inverse on inputs allowed by their stated hypotheses.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Assume a strictly positive-definite kernel on the sampled distinct locations, or formulate the projection with a Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse and restate the theorem accordingly.
issues.overall_effect: The procedure is not well defined for all advertised RKHS kernels, and the approximation and error bounds in the theorem are unsupported in that regime.
issues.title: The compression algorithm inverts a kernel matrix without ensuring invertibility
issues.why_classification: A standard local kernel condition or pseudoinverse formulation repairs the procedure without changing its rate or basic guarantee.

issues.failure_explanation: The formal result supplies only an eigenvalue-tail-dependent bound and imposes no assumptions on the locations or domain that force a Gaussian Gram matrix to have a rapidly decaying spectrum. Widely separated points can make a Gaussian Gram matrix arbitrarily close to the identity, whose eigenvalue tail does not decay rapidly. Moreover, even an exponential tail in $S$ becomes a rate in approximately $m/\log m$, not the advertised $m$, because the theorem requires $m\approx S\log(S/\delta)$.

failure_location.quote: For typical choices of the spatial kernel such as Gaussian RBF, this decay is exponential in $m$ \cite{SparseNystromCurrVar}

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: No complete source-supported repair identified; at minimum, a repair must impose and verify geometric or spectral hypotheses giving a Gaussian-kernel eigenvalue-tail bound and then translate that bound correctly through $m\approx S\log(S/\delta)$, or withdraw the explicit exponential-in-$m$ guarantee.
issues.overall_effect: The introduction's explicit exponential rate and the paper's repeated claim of theoretically guaranteed rapid error decay are not established over the advertised setting.
issues.title: The claimed exponential-in-sample-size convergence does not follow from the eigenvalue bound
issues.why_classification: The unsupported claim is the paper's principal advertised theoretical rate; the available theorem supports only a data-dependent spectral bound, so repair either needs substantial new analysis and hypotheses or loses the central exponential guarantee.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: which is a consistent approximation \cite{NCpaper}, as the edge-lengths tend to zero.

issues.failure_explanation: The compression theorem bounds error relative to a finite Dirac target. The source separately describes the edge-center normal-cycle discretization only as asymptotically consistent, and gives no mesh-size hypothesis or combined compression-plus-discretization estimate to the normal cycle of an underlying continuum shape. Thus small compression error alone does not guarantee small distance to that true normal cycle.

failure_location.quote: our compression comes with fast error decay, and guarantees of small RKHS distance to the normal cycle of the true underlying shape.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Either weaken the conclusion to accuracy relative to the discretized Dirac representation, or add a quantitative consistency theorem and combine its mesh error with the compression error by a triangle inequality.
issues.overall_effect: The conclusion materially overstates the target of the proved guarantee: the established bound concerns the chosen discrete surrogate, not the unknown underlying shape.
issues.title: The conclusion claims accuracy to the true underlying shape without a corresponding bound
issues.why_classification: A comparable discrete-target guarantee survives, but retaining the stated continuum-shape guarantee requires a nontrivial additional consistency result.
